entry: Cultural and commercial history of the lands around the [[Mediterranean Sea]]. The sea linked three continents and was the central route for transport, trade and cultural exchange. Paleolithic sites in Europe, including Orce in Spain and Kozarnika in Bulgaria, lie around its basin, and stone tools on [[Crete]] dated to 130,000 years BC indicate early use of boats. Urban civilization emerged first in Southwest Asia, at sites such as [[Çatalhöyük]], and later in Egypt and Mesopotamia. The [[Black Sea]] area is a cradle of European civilization; Solnitsata is believed to be the oldest town in Europe, and the Varna Necropolis holds what may be the earliest "well-dated" gold artifacts. In the 2nd millennium BC the Hittite and Egyptian empires competed for control of the [[Levant]]. Between 1206 and 1150 BC, the [[Bronze Age]] collapse destroyed cities from [[Troy]] to Gaza. The [[Iron Age]] brought Phoenician expansion from the Levant across the sea.

Region of southwestern Asia and North Africa that was one of the cradles of civilization. After the [[Neolithic Revolution]] and the adoption of agriculture, many of the world's oldest cultures arose here. The Sumerians were among the first to develop a civilization, around the 5th millennium BC, and Egypt was unified under its first pharaoh by 3150 BC. Assyria lasted for 1,500 years, and from the 7th century BC Persian powers such as the [[Achaemenid Empire]] dominated the region. The [[Roman Republic]] conquered most of it in the 1st century BC. From the 7th century AD, [[Islam]] spread rapidly, and the [[Ottoman Empire]] captured [[Constantinople]] in 1453. Oil discoveries in Persia (1908) and Bahrain (1932) increased Western interest. The United Nations voted in 1947 for a plan to partition Palestine, and Israel became independent in 1948. Later events included the 1967 Six-Day War, the 1973 [[OPEC]] oil embargo, the [[Iranian Revolution]] and the Arab Spring of the early 2010s.

Historical account of the [[Peloponnesian War]] (431–404 BC) by [[Thucydides]], an Athenian historian who also served as a general in the war. The work, apparently unfinished, ends mid-sentence in 411 BC and was divided into eight books by later scholars. It is regarded as one of the earliest scholarly works of history. Thucydides recorded events year by year, each year divided into a summer campaign season and a quieter winter, a method that contrasts with [[Herodotus]]. He used extensive speeches, including the funeral oration of [[Pericles]] in Book 2, which classicists doubt reproduce the words actually spoken. Scholars disagree on bias. J. B. Bury saw an objective, scientific work, while Ernst Badian argued for a strong pro-Athenian bias. Others read the work as literature, a view advanced by W. R. Connor.

headword: History of the People's Republic of China
entry: Political history of mainland China under Communist Party rule since 1949. On October 1, 1949, [[Mao Zedong]] proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen, after the Communist Party's victory in the [[Chinese Civil War]]. Land reform included state-tolerated executions of between 1 and 2 million landlords. The [[Great Leap Forward]] industrialization drive caused an estimated 15 to 55 million deaths between 1959 and 1961, mostly from starvation. The [[Cultural Revolution]], launched in 1966, brought a decade of political upheaval. After [[Deng Xiaoping]] took power in 1978, reform and opening up transformed the economy, and China's economy grew sevenfold under Jiang Zemin. [[Hong Kong]] and Macau returned in 1997 and 1999 as special administrative regions under the principle of one country, two systems. China joined the [[World Trade Organization]] in 2001. [[Xi Jinping]], paramount leader since 2012, has consolidated power through an anti-corruption campaign.

Political and cultural history of the Philippine archipelago from early settlement to independence in 1946. Human activity on the islands dates to at least 709,000 years ago. Seafaring Austronesians, who form most of the current population, migrated south from Taiwan by around 3000 BCE. From the 1st millennium, small maritime states traded with [[China]], India, [[Japan]], Thailand and Vietnam, and some were influenced by larger empires such as the [[Ming dynasty]], [[Majapahit]] and Brunei. The first recorded European visit was [[Ferdinand Magellan]]'s expedition, which landed in 1521; Magellan was killed in a battle against Lapulapu of Mactan. Miguel López de Legazpi arrived from [[Mexico]] in 1565 and founded the first permanent settlement at Cebu. Spanish rule introduced Christianity and a code of law. After Spain's defeat in the [[Spanish–American War]] in 1898, the United States took control and suppressed a revolution led by Emilio Aguinaldo. Japan occupied the islands in 1942, and the Treaty of Manila in 1946 established the independent Philippine Republic.

Political and imperial history of the state formed by the union of England and Scotland in 1707. The Acts of Union of 1800 added Ireland, creating the [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland]]. After losing its American colonies, Britain built a second [[British Empire|British Empire]] in Asia and Africa. The French Revolution and Napoleonic wars from 1793 to 1815 ended with coalitions defeating [[Napoleon]]. In the [[Victorian era]], Britain dominated the world economy and . The First World War was won in alliance with France, Russia and the US, and the [[League of Nations]] was a favored project in interwar Britain. In 1922 Northern Ireland seceded from the Irish Free State and returned to the United Kingdom. From 1945 to 1950 the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] built a welfare state and created the National Health Service. The [[Suez Crisis]] of 1956 exposed Britain's loss of superpower status, and most of its possessions became independent. A 2016 referendum to leave the European Union led to [[Brexit]] in 2020.

Political and social history of the United States. Indigenous civilizations inhabited the continent for tens of thousands of years before European colonization from the late 15th century. The Thirteen Colonies won independence in a revolutionary war that began at the [[Battles of Lexington and Concord]] in 1775, and the [[United States Declaration of Independence]] followed in 1776. In 1803 the [[Louisiana Purchase]] doubled the country's size, and westward expansion, driven by [[Manifest destiny]], brought conflict with Indigenous peoples. Disputes over slavery led to the Civil War, launched in 1861. The Union's victory at the [[Battle of Gettysburg]], the deadliest battle in American military history, was a turning point, and the Confederacy's defeat led to the abolition of slavery. The [[Great Depression]] followed the 1929 Wall Street crash, and the [[New Deal]] responded. During the [[Cold War]], the United States and the Soviet Union competed in the arms race and the Space Race. The 1991 dissolution of the Soviet Union left the United States as the world's sole superpower.

Development of self-propelled road vehicles, from steam prototypes to mass-produced cars. Crude designs date to ancient and medieval times. In 1769 Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built the first steam-powered automobile capable of carrying people. The first modern car, a practical gasoline-powered automobile, was developed by [[Carl Benz]] in 1886 and was the first in series production. Ransom E. Olds pioneered the [[Assembly line|assembly line]] using [[Interchangeable parts|interchangeable parts]]. From 1913, Ford's moving assembly line allowed the price of the [[Ford Model T]] to fall by almost 50%, making it the first mass-affordable automobile.

Development of theater as an art form over roughly 2,500 years. Theater developed into an autonomous activity distinct from ritual. Athenian tragedy, a type of dance-drama, emerged in the 6th century BC and was staged in competitions held in honor of [[Dionysus]]. Playwrights [[Aeschylus]], [[Sophocles]] and [[Euripides]] shaped the form, and complete texts by all three survive. Greek theater comprised tragedy, [[Comedy]] and the satyr play. Other traditions arose independently: Sanskrit drama was codified in the Natyasastra around 200 BCE–200 CE, and Japanese Noh theater originated in the 12th century. Medieval European theater revived through church liturgical drama by 975 CE, and the first permanent public theater in Elizabethan England opened in 1576.

Evolution of travel and goods movement, from trails and animal power to powered vehicles. Early humans created tracks by carrying goods, often following trails. Animal-drawn [[Wheel|wheeled]] vehicles were probably developed in the ancient Near East in the 4th or 5th millennium BC. The [[Roman Empire]] built roads to maintain its territory. Early [[Rail transport|rail]] systems used wooden rails to carry coal from mines to rivers, and [[Cast iron|cast iron]] plates were used from the 1760s before rolled [[Wrought iron|wrought iron]] rails made them obsolete. The first passenger-carrying public railway opened at Oystermouth in 1807, using horse-drawn carriages. In 1802 Richard Trevithick built the first [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotive]] to run on smooth rails. In 1903 the [[Wright brothers]] achieved powered flight, and commercial air services followed by the 1920s.

Development of electronic games from 1950s laboratory experiments to a global entertainment industry. Games appeared in the 1950s and 1960s on minicomputers and mainframes. Spacewar! was developed in 1962 by student hobbyists at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]. The first home console, the Magnavox Odyssey, and the first arcade games, Computer Space and Pong, appeared in the early 1970s. A flood of poor and cloned games contributed to the 1983 video game crash in the United States, after which Japan's industry took leadership of the market. The [[Nintendo Entertainment System]] was released in the United States in 1985 and helped revive the sector. The [[Game Boy]] led the first major handheld consoles of the 1990s. Sony's [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] and Microsoft's [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]] followed, while Nintendo focused on gameplay with the [[Wii]] and its motion-sensing controls. From the 2000s, mobile gaming on [[Smartphone|smartphones]] grew, and free-to-play and subscription models replaced traditional revenue models.

Development of writing systems and their effects on the societies that used them. Writing evolved from proto-writing, which used ideographic and mnemonic symbols but could not fully record spoken language. Early uses included documenting agricultural transactions and contracts, before writing spread to [[Finance|finance]], [[Religion|religion]], [[Government|government]] and [[Law|law]]. [[Writing system|Writing systems]] typically have a purpose, use specific symbols on a medium, and correspond to spoken language. Engravings and cave paintings, such as those at Lascaux, show earlier symbolic activity. Before the 20th century, many theories held that [[Cuneiform]] was invented once in [[Sumer]] and spread from there. Later research recognized several independent inventions, including Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesoamerican glyphs.

[[Personality disorder]] marked by excessive attention-seeking, emotionality and desire for approval. Symptoms usually begin in [[Adolescence|adolescence]] or early adulthood and may include inappropriate seduction, rapidly shifting emotions and excessive sensitivity to criticism. Affected people often dress flamboyantly, exaggerate their difficulties and crave stimulation and social approval. Critics argue that the diagnosis lacks construct validity and may pathologize expressive behavior, particularly in women.

Indo-European people of [[Anatolia]] who formed one of the first major civilizations of the [[Bronze Age]]. The Hittites arrived in central Anatolia before 2000 BC and formed polities including Kussara and Kanesh before establishing an empire with its capital at Hattusa. The Hittite Empire peaked in the mid-14th century BC, encompassing most of Anatolia and parts of northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia. From the 15th to 13th centuries BC they contended with the [[New Kingdom of Egypt]], the Middle Assyrian Empire and the empire of Mitanni. After the [[Late Bronze Age collapse]] at the end of the 12th century, the Hittites splintered into small states, some of which survived into the 8th century BC before absorption into the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]]. The Hittite language, with the closely related Luwian, is among the oldest historically attested [[Indo-European languages]].

Ethnic group of East and Southeast Asia, classified in China as a sub-group of the Miao people. Most live in southwestern [[China]] and mainland Southeast Asian countries such as [[Vietnam]], [[Laos]], Thailand and Myanmar, with diaspora communities in the [[United States]], Australia, France and South America. The term Hmong, adopted in the 1970s, replaced the older term Miao in English usage. Chinese texts historically used only the term Miao, and it is uncertain how many of those references concerned the Hmong. In the Vietnam War era, Hmong irregular forces fought alongside U.S. and allied troops in Laos. After 1975 they faced reprisals and an exodus, and [[Refugee|refugees]] resettled through camps in Thailand. In 1994 the term was registered with the [[United Nations]].

Largest city and financial center of [[Vietnam]], formerly Saigon (pop., 2025: more than 14 million). The city contributes around a quarter of Vietnam's GDP and is its busiest international transport hub, with Tân Sơn Nhất International Airport handling nearly half of the country's international arrivals. The area was part of [[Cambodia|Cambodian]] polities until it came under the Vietnamese Nguyễn lords in 1698. It was the capital of French Cochinchina from 1862 to 1949 and of [[French Indochina]] at intervals. After the 1954 partition it became the capital of [[South Vietnam]] until North Vietnamese forces captured it, leading to a unified communist state in 1976. The city was renamed after [[Ho Chi Minh]], while Saigon remains in informal use. In 2025 the provinces of Bình Dương and Bà Rịa–Vũng Tàu were merged into the city.

Vietnamese [[Communism|communist]] revolutionary and statesman who founded the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1945. Known as Uncle Ho, he used many pseudonyms, and details of his early life are uncertain. He worked overseas from 1911, was a founding member of the French Communist Party, and founded the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in China in 1925. He founded the Viet Minh independence movement in 1941 and led the August Revolution of 1945. His government waged guerrilla warfare from 1946, leading to the [[First Indochina War]], which ended when the Viet Minh defeated the French at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954. A land reform campaign from 1953 to 1956 included executions of landowners, which he later admitted involved excesses and errors. He supported the [[Viet Cong]] insurgency in the south, and North Vietnam won the [[Vietnam War]] in 1975. He remained president and party leader until his death from heart failure. [[Ho Chi Minh City]] was renamed in his honor.

Tropical bird of the swamps, riparian forests and mangroves of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Its digestive system supports [[Fermentation|fermentation]] of plant matter, a trait otherwise known from herbivorous [[Ruminant|ruminant]] mammals and some [[Primate|primates]], making it unique among birds. Chicks have two functional claws on each wing, which help them climb back to the nest after dropping into water to escape predators. Those claws resemble the claws of [[Archaeopteryx]], but modern researchers consider them a secondary adaptation. The hoatzin is pheasant-sized, with a blue face, maroon eyes and a spiky rufous crest. It is the national bird of [[Guyana]], where it is called the Canje pheasant.

Capital of the Australian island state of [[Tasmania]], on the estuary of the River Derwent. Founded in 1804 as a British penal colony, it is Australia's second-oldest capital after [[Sydney]]. [[Whaling]] made it the Southern Ocean's main whaling port for a time. Its skyline is dominated by kunanyi / Mount Wellington, a 1,271-meter peak, and its harbor is the second-deepest natural port in the world. Hobart is the home port for Australian and French Antarctic operations. Its attractions include convict-era architecture, Salamanca Market and the Museum of Old and New Art.

Regular activity pursued for enjoyment, typically during [[Leisure|leisure]] time. Hobbies include [[Collecting|collecting]] themed items, creative and artistic pursuits, and [[Sport|sports]], and they are usually practiced for interest rather than financial reward. Hobbies follow social trends: stamp collecting was popular in the 19th and 20th centuries, while [[Video game|video games]] have gained popularity more recently. Robert Stebbins's Serious Leisure Perspective divides hobbies into casual leisure, serious leisure and project-based leisure. Hobbies gained respectability in the 18th century, as industrial society gave people more leisure time. A 2023 meta-analysis of over 93,000 older adults found that hobby engagement correlates with better self-reported health and greater life satisfaction.

Type of blood and immune-system [[Cancer|cancer]] in which Reed–Sternberg cells appear in the lymph nodes. It is named after the English physician Thomas Hodgkin, who first described it in 1832. Painless enlargement of lymph nodes in the neck, armpit or groin is common, often with fever, night sweats and weight loss. About half of cases arise from [[Epstein–Barr virus]]. Diagnosis requires a lymph node [[Biopsy|biopsy]] showing Reed–Sternberg cells. Treatment with [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]], [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] or both often cures early-stage disease.

Ancient agricultural hand tool for shaping soil, removing weeds and harvesting [[Root|root]] crops. Shaping soil includes piling earth around plants and digging narrow furrows and shallow trenches for planting [[Seed|seeds]] or bulbs. There are two general types: draw hoes, which chop into the ground and are pulled toward the user, and scuffle hoes, which scrape the surface to cut weeds. The Dutch hoe is pushed or pulled just below the surface to cut weed roots, while the ridging hoe digs the narrow furrows used for planting. Hoes for digging soil are used to harvest crops such as [[Potato|potatoes]]. Archaeological evidence traces hoe-like tools to ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt around 4000 BCE.

Second-largest of [[Japan|Japan's]] four main islands and its northernmost prefecture. Hokkaido is separated from [[Honshu]] by the Tsugaru Strait and linked to it by the Seikan Tunnel. Its capital, [[Sapporo]], is its largest city. Its northern position brings a cold climate and heavy snowfall, yet it is an agricultural breadbasket for many crops. [[Sakhalin]], in Russia, lies about 43 kilometers (27 mi) to the north, and Russia administers the Kuril Islands, the four southernmost of which Japan claims. The island was inhabited mainly by the [[Ainu people]] until Japanese settlers ruled its southern tip from the 16th century. After the [[Meiji Restoration]], Japan annexed the entire island in 1869 and renamed it Hokkaido. The Ainu lost much of their land and were largely assimilated, which has nearly erased their language and traditions.

Major Hindu festival of colors, love and spring, celebrated mainly in [[India]] and [[Nepal]]. It celebrates the love between [[Krishna|Radha and Krishna]] and commemorates the victory of [[Vishnu]] as Narasimha over Hiranyakashipu. Bonfires are lit the night before in Holika Dahan, and on the next day people throw colored water and powder at each other. The festival marks the end of winter and the arrival of spring, and invokes a good harvest. It falls on the [[Full moon|full moon]] day of the [[Hindu calendar]] month of Phalguna, typically in March. The festival is mentioned in ancient texts and by the poet Kālidāsa during the 4th-century reign of [[Chandragupta II]]. It has spread to the [[Caribbean]] and parts of the Western world.

Day or period of time set aside for [[Festival|festivals]] or [[Recreation|recreation]], by custom or by law. Public holidays are set by public authorities and vary by state or region, while religious holidays are set by religious organizations. Some, such as [[Christmas]], have become secularized and commercialized. The word comes from [[Old English]] hāligdæg, meaning "holy day". In the United States, "the holidays" usually means the period from Thanksgiving to New Year's. New Year's Day is the most common public holiday, observed in all Gregorian-calendar countries except [[Israel]]. Christmas is celebrated by over 2 billion people, and 61% of British people celebrate it in an entirely secular way. The United Nations publishes a list of International Days and Weeks.
